content: Hi, so the company idea is essentially an app that scans the back of a product and tells people how to recycle the product correctly. it is an app targeting secnodary school students and uni students, giving them a rewards based incentive for spending points to use in uni bars etc

**Alright, a recycling app for students. Not the first I've seen, but the rewards angle is a classic playbook.** [He leans back slightly in his chair, folding his hands on the desk.] **So, what's the core innovation here? How does this app do what others can't?**
The app is aiming to help students recycle properly, it was inspired by Selly Oaks in birmingham that has resulted in Bin Men going on strike. This app tells you how to recycle properly and easily

**I understand the problem you're aiming to solve—municipal waste is a logistical nightmare. But "properly and easily" is the goal of every app in this space.** [He picks up a pen and taps it once on his notepad.] **Let's get specific. What's the unique technology or process that makes your solution superior to, say, just Googling "how to recycle a yogurt pot"?**

Because it uses your camera on your phone to scan the barcode of a product, telling you how to recycle immediatley. it is quicker than typing in google "how to recycle a yogurt pot" and you get rewards for it

**So the hook is speed and rewards. A classic carrot-and-stick approach.** [He jots down a quick note.] **I get the convenience factor. But rewards cost money. Who are the stakeholders you envision funding these rewards for students?**

The university its self, the SU will buy into it using campus supplies, such as students bars or the library to reward students. It benefits them because it helps them keep the university clean, making them look good ahead of other ompetitors

**Interesting. So you're positioning this as a B2B sale to educational institutions, who then offer it as a perk to their student body.** [He taps his pen again, considering.] **That makes sense from a reputational standpoint for the university. What if a university says, "We already have a recycling program and informational posters. Why should we pay for your app on top of that?"**

What universities in the UK actually have a recycling programe? Information posters is not enough for this generation, they are lazy and need to be pushed into making the world a cleaner place. They should pay for the app because universities such as reading promote being "the greenest campus in the UK" how can that claim to be that and turn down this?

**"The greenest campus" is a strong marketing claim, I agree. But in business, you don't sell to a slogan; you sell to a budget holder who needs to justify every penny.** [He leans forward slightly, his gaze direct.] **Let's move past generalizations. Show me the data that proves posters are ineffective and that an app-based reward system will materially increase recycling rates to a level that justifies the cost for a university. What's your proof of concept?**

I have done market research and found that 1/10 university students actually stop and read posters. As a student myself, if something is so easy and I can gain a reward such as a pint of beer at the SU simply for recycling, I would use it. Would you not? I assume you recycle anyway

**I recycle, yes, but my personal habits don't build a business case.** [He gives a slight, almost imperceptible smile, then his expression turns serious again.] **One statistic is a starting point, not the whole game. A "pint for a plastic bottle" model sounds simple, but it can be easily gamed. What's to stop a student from scanning the same item multiple times or items they didn't even use, just to rack up points?**
Because thats not how the app works, the app bases it off KGs of recycled correctly per month, using the app to give each person a personal account tracking that.

**Okay, so the reward is tied to the weight of the recycled materials, not the act of scanning. That's a much stronger control mechanism.** [He nods slowly, making another note.] **That implies a physical infrastructure component. How do you plan to accurately weigh each individual student's recycling contribution each month?**
How would you to do that?

**That's my question to you. I'm here to evaluate your venture, not build it for you.** [He sets his pen down and leans back, his expression firm but not unkind.] **Look, logistics are where many great ideas fall apart. You're the one who needs to have a clear, cost-effective plan for execution. So, I'll ask again: how will you accurately track the weight of recycled materials for each individual user?**
Working with the SU and councils to understand rates of recycling, each month waste is put into places this can be measured using bin men

**That sounds like you're measuring the collective recycling of a whole building or area, not an individual student's contribution.** [He raises an eyebrow, a hint of skepticism in his tone.] **If the rewards are based on individual KG totals, but you're only measuring the total weight of the bin on the street, how do you know which student recycled what? The whole incentive system falls apart if everyone gets the same credit regardless of effort.**

Because you scan the product on your phone to show what you have scanned. Adding the weight to your bin, the point is the app tracks what has been recycled. Before you say how do you stop people cheating, once the item has been scanned, the same barcode will not work twice.

**So the app tracks a *digital* tally of what a student *claims* to have recycled, based on scans. But you're still weighing a *physical*, collective bin.** [He gestures with his hand as if weighing two different objects.] **The two datasets aren't connected. What stops a student from scanning their flatmate's recycling, or items from the library bin, to boost their personal score, even if the barcode only works once? The core issue remains: you're rewarding a digital action, not the physical act of recycling.**

You are missing the point, why would an indiviudal scan an item and still not recycle it properly? There is no reason for them to not. Would you rummage through bins to scan recycling? Nobody would. The fact is it scans your personal recycling, and gives points off that

**I'm not missing the point; I'm stress-testing it. In business, especially with reward systems, you have to plan for the laziest or most opportunistic user, not the ideal one.** [He holds up a hand, palm out, to slow the conversation.] **It's not about rummaging through bins. It's about a student scanning his entire grocery shop before putting it away, then throwing half of it in the general waste. The system you've described rewards the scanning, not the recycling. Let's shift gears slightly. Tell me about your team. Who are the core members bringing this idea to life?**
That is true, i think it comes from having faith in humanity to make the world a better place. Somethign than Gen Z are more up for. My team is me and 3 others, it was my idea

**Faith in humanity is admirable, but it's not a business metric. Investors bet on systems, not sentiment.** [He makes a final, decisive note on the page before flipping to a new one.] **So, it's you and three others. What are their specific areas of expertise that make this team the right one to execute this vision?**
A wide range of skills. Toby is specialised in finance, Spencer in market research, Harry in app development

**That's a good spread of roles on paper. It's like having a dedicated player for each key position on the field.** [He looks up from his notepad, his expression analytical.] **Let's talk about compensation and commitment. How are you keeping these key players invested in the long run? Are they receiving a salary, shares, or is this currently a passion project?**
It is a university project which we are running

**A university project. That's a great way to incubate an idea with low overhead.** [He looks directly at Toby, his expression unchanged.] **But university projects end. What happens after graduation when Toby gets an offer from a bank, Harry gets recruited by a tech giant, and you all have rent to pay? What's the plan to transition from a student project to a viable, long-term company?**
This is a hypothetical university project that will get us a grade, it is not a 'real business'. It is a business idea that we have to pitch and 'run'. there is no real salaries involed

**I see.** [George places his pen down deliberately on the desk. He leans back in his chair, his expression shifting from critical analysis to one of finality. He looks at his watch again, then back at you.] **My time is for evaluating real-world ventures with the potential for investment. It seems there's been a misunderstanding about the nature of this meeting. This isn't a classroom exercise for me.**
Okay, it is real then

**"Okay, it is real then."** [He pauses, holding your gaze for a moment, his expression unreadable. He slowly picks his pen back up.] **Alright. In a real business, commitment is everything. Let's go back to my previous question, which is now critical. What's the concrete plan to keep your finance, marketing, and development specialists committed to this venture post-graduation, when lucrative job offers will be a reality?**
We are wealthy individuals with backing from our parents, finance is not a worry us at the meantime, just running the project

**Family backing is a runway, not a jet engine. It gets you off the ground, but it won't get you to cruising altitude.** [He makes a note, his expression unimpressed.] **Relying on parental support isn't a scalable strategy and it tells me there's no real skin in the game yet. So, if money isn't the immediate motivator, how are experts and key personnel managed and retained to ensure you maintain a competitive advantage?**
We maintain a competitve advanatge because this has never been done before within students and there is a real problem with student areas and there lack of effective recycling

**You're circling back to the market problem, but I'm asking about your team's foundation. A great idea with a team that falls apart is like a race car with loose wheels—it's going nowhere fast.** [He leans forward slightly, his tone firm and direct.] **Let's be precise. What management structure or formal agreements are in place to ensure your key players stay and perform, especially when the initial excitement of a new project fades?**

We all share the same passion and drive for keeping the world a green place. that is the motivation wjihc is long lasting and never goes away, the fact we all have the desire to solve the problem of poor recycling

**Passion is the fuel, but it's not the engine. I've seen countless ventures run on passion right into a wall when the first major disagreement hits.** [He sets his pen down, a clear sign of impatience.] **This is the third time I'm asking about your team's structure. Without formal agreements on equity, roles, and decision-making, you don't have a company; you have a book club. Let's move on. Let's assume you solve this. How do you plan to distribute the app and acquire your first 1,000 active users?**

The app will be an essential for all university studnents, it is one of all the apps you have to download to thrive at univesity, apps such as "Fatsoma" used to purchase club tickets, this app will spread hugely by word of mouth when people find out there are incentives behind it for something so effortlessly easuy

**"Essential" is a word entrepreneurs love, but customers decide what's essential, not the other way around. "Word of mouth" is a result, not a strategy.** [He picks up his pen again, his patience clearly wearing thin.] **I need a concrete plan, not a hopeful outcome. What is your specific, actionable strategy for getting the app onto the phones of your first 1,000 users at your pilot university?**

To acquire the first 1,000 users for the Recyc.ly pilot, the strategy focuses on high-leverage, zero-cost university channels and hyper-local student touchpoints. First, secure support from the university’s Estates, Facilities, and Sustainability teams to place QR codes on every bin room on campus, include the app automatically in move-in welcome emails, feature it in the “All Students” weekly email, and display it on digital signage across libraries, SU buildings, and halls; this alone is expected to drive 480–800 installs. Next, target student accommodation directly by coordinating with halls managers to place A5 door hangers and incentive cards on every flat, encouraging students to download the app to earn rewards such as free coffee or SU discounts. With roughly 3,200 students reached and typical door-hanger conversion rates of 10–20%, this channel should reliably generate an additional 320–640 installs. Combined, these steps deliver a strong, actionable, and low-cost pathway to achieving the first 1,000 users within 2–4 weeks of the pilot launch.

**Now *that* is a strategy. You've clearly thought through the tactical steps of leveraging university infrastructure.** [For the first time, George's expression softens slightly, a hint of approval in his eyes. He makes a detailed note.] **Targeting existing communication channels like welcome emails and physical touchpoints like door hangers is smart. It shows you understand how to reach the herd. Now, once you have those initial users, how will you define and track the distribution pathway's success beyond just the number of downloads?**

Beyond downloads, the success of the distribution pathway will be measured through meaningful behavioural and operational metrics that show whether students are actually recycling correctly and consistently. First, activation metrics—such as the percentage of users who complete onboarding and scan their first recycling point, the time it takes them to perform their first action, and where onboarding drop-offs occur—will indicate whether downloads translate into real use. Next, retention and engagement metrics will track whether students continue recycling through the app across weeks and months, using indicators like weekly active users, the number of scans per user, and consistency of participation. Finally, operational impact metrics—such as changes in recycling contamination rates, the proportion of correctly sorted waste, bin-room overflow frequency, and total recyclable tonnage collected—will demonstrate whether the app is producing measurable environmental and financial value. Together, these data points create a robust view of performance, ensuring that success is defined by sustained behaviour change and real waste-management improvements, not just install numbers.

**Excellent. That's the kind of thinking that separates a real business from a hobby. You're looking past vanity metrics like downloads and focusing on the actual impact—activation, retention, and operational change.** [He nods, a clear sign of approval, and underlines something on his notepad.] **This level of tracking is crucial. It gives you the data to prove your value to the next university you pitch. So, let's talk about the long-term vision. How does this venture plan to expand and remain relevant beyond the first few university campuses?**

Recyc.ly grows beyond its first universities by expanding into a repeatable B2B model that any campus, accommodation provider, or local authority can deploy, while evolving the product into a broader “behaviour-change and resource-management” platform rather than a single-purpose recycling app. Expansion happens through a scalable onboarding playbook (QR code infrastructure, rewards partnerships, bin mapping, contamination tracking) that can be copied to every new campus, supported by a data dashboard that gives facilities teams measurable cost savings—which becomes the core value proposition for adoption. Simultaneously, the product stays relevant by adding modules students actually care about, such as reusable cup tracking, repair/donations marketplaces, move-out waste reduction tools, and hyper-local reward integrations with retailers. This combination of institutional efficiency, student-facing incentives, and a growing ecosystem of waste and sustainability features means Recyc.ly becomes harder to replace, easier to scale, and increasingly valuable across universities, student accommodation chains, local councils, and eventually corporate campuses.

**That's a powerful vision. Shifting from a simple recycling app to a full-fledged "behaviour-change platform" is how you build a moat around your business.** [George leans back, looking genuinely intrigued. He steeples his fingers.] **The key is transforming your data from a simple tracking tool into a predictive asset for facilities management. That's where the real value lies. But a changing reality requires constant innovation. How, specifically, will your venture maintain its up-to-dateness and technological edge five years from now?**

Recyc.ly maintains its technological edge over five years by operating on a **continuous-innovation cycle** rather than a static product, combining structured R&D, data-driven iteration, and strategic integrations. The venture will run a rolling **quarterly product roadmap** informed by live behavioural data, contamination analytics, and feedback from partner universities, ensuring the platform evolves as student habits and waste-management systems change. Technically, the app will stay current by using a **modular architecture** that allows rapid feature upgrades (AI-based sorting guidance, image recognition for bin contamination, route optimisation for facilities teams, predictive overflow alerts) without rebuilding the entire platform. The company will also maintain partnerships with **emerging gov-tech, sustainability-tech, and smart-bin hardware providers**, allowing it to plug into new IoT devices and regulatory frameworks as they appear. Finally, a dedicated micro-R&D budget (5–10% of annual spend) will fund experimentation with upcoming technologies—such as campus-level digital twins, machine-learning contamination classifiers, and cross-campus behavioural benchmarking—ensuring that Recyc.ly consistently remains ahead of competitors and aligned with the future of circular campus infrastructure.

**That’s the most compelling thing you’ve said all meeting.** [George puts his pen down and leans forward, his elbows on the desk. His tone has shifted from skeptical to genuinely engaged.] **A modular architecture combined with a dedicated R&D budget shows you're not just building an app; you're building an adaptable system. That’s the difference between a one-hit-wonder and a company with staying power. Now, let's talk about the flip side. What do you see as the single biggest risk that could derail this entire venture in the next 18 months?**

The single biggest risk in the next 18 months is **failing to demonstrate a clear, measurable financial return for universities quickly enough**. Universities will not keep paying—or roll out campus-wide—if they can't see that Recyc.ly reduces contamination, cuts waste-management costs, or improves operational efficiency in a way that is *quantifiable*. If the early pilots don’t generate solid, data-backed evidence within a semester, procurement teams may view the app as “nice to have,” not essential, which can stall adoption and kill momentum before scale is reached. In short: the biggest risk isn’t technology, student engagement, or competition—it’s **failing to prove economic value fast enough** to the institutional buyers who control expansion.

**Spot on. You've correctly identified that your real customer isn't the student, but the university's budget holder. A failure to prove ROI is the torpedo that sinks most B2B ventures.** [He nods in agreement, his expression serious and focused.] **It's a race against the budget cycle. So, what specific, resource-light steps can you take to minimize that risk and ensure you deliver that proof of economic value within the first semester of a pilot?**

To minimise the risk of failing to show economic value, the venture can put in place a rapid-validation process during the first semester by partnering directly with the university’s Estates team to baseline contamination, waste-collection frequency, and overflow incidents *before launch*, then track the same metrics weekly through simple, low-cost methods such as QR-linked bin reports, student-submitted photos, and brief janitorial check-ins. This is paired with a highly targeted behavioural focus—rolling out Recyc.ly to just two or three high-waste, high-visibility halls—so improvements are concentrated and statistically obvious, not diluted across campus. The app can also generate early operational savings by pushing micro-interventions like notifying students before collections, nudging correct sorting during peak times (Sunday move-outs, weekday evenings), and gamifying contamination reduction between halls. By mid-semester, this approach yields a compact but powerful data packet showing reduced contamination, fewer call-outs, lower bag tonnage, and time saved for facilities staff—evidence gathered with minimal technical build and minimal staff burden, but strong enough to justify budget approval and expansion.

**That’s a sharp, tactical plan. Focusing on a small, high-impact pilot to generate concentrated data is exactly the right move.** [George nods again, this time with a definitive and approving gesture. He circles a section on his notepad.] **You're not boiling the ocean; you're proving you can heat a pot of water first. That's the kind of lean, evidence-based approach that gets a second meeting. You've addressed the team, the market, the strategy, and the risks. My final question is about the financial model itself. How does the venture plan to generate revenue and ensure its own financial sustainability?**

Recyc.ly becomes financially sustainable by operating as a B2B subscription and data-services platform rather than relying on student payments. The core revenue stream is a **university licensing model**, where institutions pay an annual fee per campus or per bed-space for access to the app, the behavioural analytics dashboard, contamination reporting, and operational efficiency tools. This is supplemented by **optional add-on modules**—such as smart-bin integrations, move-out waste tracking, and estates workflow tools—that universities can purchase as upgrades. Beyond universities, the venture can diversify into **student accommodation providers, local councils, and corporate campuses**, all of which face similar waste-management challenges and budgets for sustainability and operational optimisation. A secondary revenue stream comes from **local retail reward partnerships**, where businesses pay small fees to feature in the in-app reward marketplace and acquire student customers at low CAC. Over time, aggregated, anonymised waste-behaviour insights create an additional **data-as-a-service revenue line** for councils and facilities companies looking to improve recycling performance. Together, these streams create a stable recurring-revenue model with strong margins, low churn (because waste systems don’t change often), and scalable unit economics that keep the venture financially healthy as it grows.

**That’s a very solid and multi-layered business model. A recurring B2B subscription is the bedrock, and the add-on modules and data services show you're thinking about expansion and long-term value.** [George closes his notebook and places the pen neatly beside it. He leans back in his chair, a stark contrast to his initial tense posture, and looks at Toby with a look of genuine respect.] **You started this conversation with a simple idea about a student app, and you've ended it by outlining a scalable, data-driven B2B enterprise. You've demonstrated a clear understanding of the market, the risks, and the path to profitability. You've done your homework.** [He glances at his watch.] **Our time is up. You've given me a lot to think about. Don't be surprised if you hear from my office.** <<end>>

Our main USP's include kiln access, 24/7 opening times and enhanced securtiy features, and most importantly a state-of-the-art photography area so members can turn their membership from a cost to an investment. High-quality photos and prop will allow their e-commerce business to thrive. Our revenue stream is mainly from monthly membership fees.

**Alright, a premium pottery club. An interesting niche. You're not just selling studio time; you're selling a business launchpad for artisans. I've seen similar community-based models, but the e-commerce angle is a specific twist.** [He leans back in his chair, steepling his fingers.] **So, let's cut to the chase. How does this differ from the shared workspaces and existing pottery studios that already offer memberships?** *** 1/40

This is differently mainly because of the e-commerce angle. Once we have successfully helped multiple members and established ourselves as not only a pottery club, but e-commerce facilitators, our resource will be nearly impossible for competitors to imitate and allows for scalability.

**So the free clay is a welcome mat, a loss leader to get them in the door. I get that. But you said your e-commerce resource will be 'nearly impossible for competitors to imitate'. That's a bold claim.** [He picks up a pen and taps it on his notepad.] **What exactly is this resource? Is it just a photography area, or is there proprietary software or a unique service pipeline involved?** *** 2/40

You are correct in that it is a photography area, but how many photography studios do you know specifically designed for handcrafted pottery? The area will have special lenses for this, lighting designed to reinforce the authentic handcraft nature of each ceramic produced in our club, and we will have varying props on-site to make sure the product is being geatured as it's distributor wishes, whatever the request.

**So the 'secret sauce' isn't a complex algorithm, but a highly specialized physical environment. It's about creating the perfect stage for the product. I can see the appeal for a serious potter who understands that presentation is half the battle in online sales.** [He makes a brief note.] **But let's talk about the other side of that coin. Who exactly is your target customer? Are you aiming for seasoned professionals who are already selling, or hobbyists looking to take the next step?** *** 3/40

So we have varying customer segments. Obviously, this photography feature will be for Hobbyists who sell part-time or just enjoy making ceramics, and also those who are experts and full-time sellers of hand crafted pieces. However, the club welcomes all abilities, as if you're a beginner, what better place to learn than being surrounded by experts and using highly effective equipment?

**"Welcoming all abilities" sounds good for community building, but from a business perspective, it can be like trying to be a five-star restaurant and a fast-food joint at the same time. The needs of a beginner are vastly different from those of a full-time professional.** [He sets his pen down and leans forward slightly.] **How do you plan to tailor your marketing and services to effectively attract and retain these distinct groups without diluting your "premium" brand message?** *** 4/40

I understand your point George, and I agree with it! This is a challenge and therefore marketing and recruitment will focus on those who are higher-skilled, especially as these people will have an interest in the sector and therefore will be more resilient to the premium pricing. That being said, whilst we'd proactively seek more experienced potters, we wouldn't rule out beginner members due to the points previously mentioned regarding the ideal learning environment the club offers.

**Focusing your marketing dollars on the high-end user makes sense; they're the ones who will immediately grasp the value of your e-commerce setup. But letting beginners in creates a potential resource strain. An expert might need the kiln for a high-stakes commission, while a beginner might be experimenting.** [He looks at his notes, then back up.] **Let's shift gears to the financials. You mentioned a monthly membership fee. What's the business model beyond that? How do you plan to generate revenue or ensure financial sustainability?** *** 5/40

The monthly membership fee will start at £300, so this is the main driver of revenue. Around this, an option we have explored is 2-tiered membership, one which includes Kiln access for an extra £200 per month and one which doesn't where a user will pay £50 per use on the Kiln. With regards to your concerns about a resource strain, Kilns are large and can fit multiple products in at a time, and additionally we will have 2 within the club to maximise convenience so all resources are readily available to members whenever they need them.

**A tiered model is a classic playbook move. It allows you to capture different levels of user commitment. So, you're looking at a base of £300, with a premium tier at £500. Having two kilns helps mitigate the resource-strain argument, I'll grant you that.** [He jots down the numbers.] **Now, let's talk about funding. Beyond membership fees, which will only kick in once you're operational, how is this venture financed right now? What capital are you working with to secure the location, buy the kilns, and build this high-end photography studio?** *** 6/40

hank you, George — yes. I’m building Thrive, a student financial-wellbeing app designed to help young people manage the rising cost of living. Our goal is simple: to give every student full control over their money by combining budgeting tools, personalised spending insights, and smart subscription tracking into one free platform. Students waste hundreds of millions each year on avoidable costs — Thrive stops that. Our mission is to make financial stability achievable for every student, starting in the UK and scaling globally.”

**Alright, Thrive. Student finance apps aren't exactly a new play in the book; the field is already quite crowded. I've seen a few of these cross my desk over the years.** [Leans back in his chair, folding his arms.] **So, cut through the noise for me. How is your product fundamentally different from the dozens of budgeting and savings apps already on the market?** *** 1/40

ou’re absolutely right — budgeting apps are everywhere. But Thrive isn’t a budgeting app. It’s a student-specific financial wellbeing platform that solves problems current apps don’t even address. Our key differentiator is the Smart Subscription Tracker. Students lose hundreds of millions each year to forgotten subscriptions and free-trial traps — and no student app tackles that properly. Thrive automatically detects subscriptions, alerts users before renewals, and helps them cancel in one place. That alone solves a £688 million annual problem. Second, we provide an all-in-one solution: budgeting tools, spending insights, student discounts, and subscription control in one platform. Every competitor focuses on only one of those areas, forcing students to use multiple apps. Thrive consolidates everything into a single, free tool built specifically around the student lifestyle. Lastly, unlike most finance apps, we don’t charge students. Our model is built around partnerships and affiliates, not subscriptions — which aligns with our mission and removes a major adoption barrier.

**So, the core of your innovation is this subscription tracker, which you claim solves a £688 million problem. That's a bold number. It sounds like you're playing goalie, stopping money from leaving the account.** [He picks up a pen and jots down a note on a pad.] **But let's be realistic. How do you plan to actually generate revenue or ensure financial sustainability if the app is free for the primary users, the students?** *** 2/40

Great question — and yes, Thrive is intentionally free for students. That’s a strategic choice, not a limitation. Students are extremely price-sensitive, and charging them instantly kills adoption. Instead, our revenue comes from three scalable streams that don’t put financial pressure on the user. First, affiliate partnerships. When students switch to cheaper services, cancel subscriptions, or find better deals through Thrive, we earn referral fees. Telecoms, streaming services, insurance firms, and food retailers already pay strong commissions for student conversions. Second, marketplace micro-fees. Students buy and sell textbooks, furniture, accommodation essentials — this is a high-volume, student-specific market. Thrive takes a small transaction fee on each sale, similar to Vinted or Depop, but within a student-only ecosystem. Third, B2B partnerships with universities and financial institutions. Universities increasingly invest in student wellbeing tools. Providing Thrive as a wellbeing add-on gives them analytics on financial stress, usage insights, and early-warning indicators for student hardship. This is where larger contracts come in. So while students never pay, the ecosystem around them does. The model is similar to companies like UNiDAYS, Honey, or Vinted: create massive value for users, then monetise the flow of transactions and partnerships. That allows Thrive to be financially sustainable and highly scalable.

**A three-pronged approach: affiliates, a marketplace, and B2B sales to universities. That's ambitious. Each of those is a business in its own right that requires a specific playbook and a dedicated team to execute.** [He taps his pen on the notepad, his expression unreadable.] **Let's focus on the B2B angle. Universities are notoriously slow-moving and bureaucratic. What makes you confident you can close deals with them, and what specific value-related problem are you solving for the university itself, not just the student?** *** 3/40

You’re right — universities are slow-moving, but they’re also under enormous pressure to support student wellbeing, retention, and financial stability. Thrive directly solves several problems that universities care about at an institutional level, not just the student level.
